doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

title: Studio records versus live shows
summary: Fleck says the records are a more refined counterpart to live shows, which fans may tape. Songs sometimes come together only in the studio after many takes.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Do you ever have trouble when you’re doing studio recordings knowing when to stop? Knowing when something is actually finished?

Yeah. I don’t know. I mean when I listen back to the records they don’t sound warmed over to me. That would be the worry is that they were too slick or that there wasn’t any life to them or something. Because I mean you know it’s like, I don’t know, there are some artists you see paintings and they’re real rough and wild and the mis- — I don’t want to call them mistakes — but the roughness is part of the greatness of it, and there’s other painters who paint so fine it’s like a photograph and it’s so perfect and you love that about their work. I mean it’s the prerogative of the artist to decide whether he wants his stuff to be like a really fine hundred year old bottle of wine or something newer that’s a little rougher. I don’t know. There’s a lot of ways to describe it, whether you like really smooth silk or whether you like something, or a rough sweater or something. I mean they’re both good, it’s just, so I think with the Flecktones we’re trying to — and also I think about the records in the studios as offsetting the live shows which we allow people to tape and distribute. That’s the total, what we sound like live in person. That, everybody can check that out for free, that’s out there. So we want the record to be different from that. We want it to be a more refined version of it. We want to use the records as a way to improve as musicians and to practice the music. A lot of times when you’re recording you don’t know the song that well so it’s not like a performance where usually not only have you played the song enough to perform it in public but you’re playing to an audience that’s inspiring you to like make sure you really do it right. When you’re in the studio sitting around with the guys it’s different. And to get up to that level of intensity, © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

you might need to do it twenty times. Plus there’s part of these songs that are hard and that’s the time that the songs sometimes really come together is in the studio. So it’s just part of the whole picture. It’s like a postcard and then there’s the everyday — we play this song at the show and how it changes. And sometimes we never play it as good as we got it on the record. Sometimes we never get it on the record because we do it live.
